Notes: Year Established -90 = midpoint of the Hasmonean period (140-37 BCE): the earliest datable evidence of Jewish residents is a burial cave found at Jifna in 1995 whose excavation yielded potsherds typical of the Hasmonean, Herodian and early Roman periods, used until the Bar Kokhba revolt (Zelinger 2001, as cited by the page). Scholars argue Gophna was only founded in the Second Temple period (Robinson's identification with Ophni of Benjamin is rejected). Earlier mention not used as a row: Josephus (War 1.45) says Judas Maccabaeus fled 'to the toparchy of Gophna' after a defeat by Antiochus V (c. 162 BCE) - this documents the rebel army in the district, not residents of the town. Presence row: Jewish burial = local Jewish community, scale unknown.

Event: Cassius (c. 43 BCE) 'reduced four cities into a state of slavery, the two most potent of which were Gophna and Emmaus' and Lydda and Thamna, for delay in paying tribute (Josephus, Antiquities 14.11.2 / 14.275; parallel War 1.222). Shows Gophna as a leading Jewish town of Judea by the mid-1st c. BCE. No count of inhabitants given; Population blank (not 0: they were freed shortly after).

Event: c. 42-41 BCE Mark Antony freed the inhabitants of Gofnah whom Cassius had sold into slavery for unpaid taxes (Encyclopaedia Judaica 'Gofnah'); implies the Jewish community returned. The entry also notes the Talmud calls Gofnah a 'city of priests' (Ber. 44a; y. Ta'an. 4:8) - legendary/undated, not used as a row.

Event: in the time of Herod (37-4 BCE; midpoint -20) Gofnah replaced Timnah as the center of a toparchy of Judea and kept this position later (Encyclopaedia Judaica, citing Josephus War 1.45, 3.55 and Pliny NH 5.15/5.70). Administrative capital of a Jewish district; no population figure.

Presence: ossuary inscribed in Hebrew 'Bilga' (name of the 10th priestly course), dated 63 BCE-70 CE (early Roman midpoint 4 CE, c.), listed under Gophna in the Corpus/Inscriptions of Israel/Palestine database (Sukenik 1933, 'An Ancient Jewish Cave on the Jerusalem-Shechem Road'); no provenance given, so attribution to Gophna itself is per the database only. Suggests a priestly Jewish family.

Event: at the outbreak of the Great Revolt (66 CE) the rebel government made 'John, the son of Matthias' (other MSS/translations: son of Ananias) governor of the toparchies of Gophnitica (text 'Gophritica') and Acrabattene (Josephus, War 2.20.4 / 2.568). Encyclopaedia Judaica names the commander Hananiah b. Johanan. Gophna district under Jewish rebel administration; no figure.

Presence/administration: Josephus' description of Judea (War 3.3.5 / 3.55, written in the context of the war, c. 67 CE): after Jerusalem 'Gophna was the second of those cities' (toparchy capitals), followed by Acrabatta, Thamna, Lydda, Emmaus etc. Indicates Gophna as a major Jewish town and district seat; no population figure. Pliny NH 5.70 (c. 77 CE, outside the period) also lists the toparchy of 'Gophnah'.

Event: in 68 CE the Roman commander (Vespasian) 'went up to the mountainous country, and took those two toparchies that were called the Gophnitick and Acrabattene toparchies' (Josephus, War 4.9.9 / 4.551). Per Encyclopaedia Judaica he occupied Gofnah and placed a garrison there. Not stated that the Jewish inhabitants were removed; Population blank.
Event: in spring 70 CE Titus 'marched through Samaria to Gophna, a city that had been formerly taken by his father' and then held by a Roman garrison (Josephus, War 5.2.1 / 5.50).

Event: during the siege of Jerusalem (summer 70 CE) Titus sent the chief priests and nobles who had deserted to him to Gophna, 'knowing they would not willingly live after the customs of other nations', to remain there until the war ended (Josephus, War 6.2.2 / 6.115; recalled in 6.118 to show themselves at the walls). A temporary group of Jewish refugees/deserters (Josephus names several high-priestly families), not a resident count; Population blank. Implies Gophna remained a place where Jews could live by Jewish custom.
